about.0:
GOETHE’S SUN - In the introduction to his well
known 1810 Farbenlehre (Theory of Colours),
Goethe establishes an analogy between eye and
sun. Departing from the theories on the ancient
world, he never ceased to say again and again that
only like can understand like and that there’s no
one that would deny this direct affinity between
eye and light; just as the words of an old mystic,
which in German rhymes can be thus expressed:
If the eye didn’t have the sun,
How should we see the light?
Without the strength of God among us,
How are we seduced by the divine?

The German poet echoes the Greek tradition that
since Empedocles saw such analogy between
what’s perceived and the organ that perceives.
This Aristotle characterizes, in De Anima, as a
knowledge of the resembling to the resemblant;
a tradition that would later be reworked by Plotinus during the Renaissance. Thus, the touch was
related to the earth, the hearing to the air, the
wet water with taste and, at last, the brightest
sense, vision, with sunlight. The eye converts in
the sun so it may reflect the universe. (...)
In “Goethe’s Sun” (1990), Barja goes back to an
ancient relation, to the ancient will of finding
relations, always seductive, between music and
light. (...) To look with attention is, thus, also to listen, since the look that sees no doubt also speaks
and hears; thus producing and endless game of
interchange between vision and ear, between
the words that are seen and the images that are
heard. Reciprocity of the senses, of the images
and words, also of feelings and places. It’s not
about excluding the perception of sensitivity but
to verify that there is an unfolding of sensibility
through another way of feeling. “what is it to see
that may also be heard?“
Mercedez Replinger extract from the book Instalações
Barja  - 2005 / “The language of seeing”/ Marisa Flórido.

They are characters to be recombined in this vast and mundane library. He selects them and associates them in improbable connections, at times laughable parodies that show the arbitrariness of signs and discourses, the blind spots that always take the arts by assault, the illegibilities that haunt them. References that initially seemed odd to us start being stitched, connected, producing new meanings, new abysses. John the Baptist meets another John, Beuys; the sun/ eye of Goethe turns into the fifth musical note of the C scale opening itself to the ears; the eye, knowledge’s and vertical transcendence’s privileged organ (from Plato’s sun to the divine light) converts into Bataille’s anus-eye. In the interval between visible and invisible, what is said and what is silenced, revelation and blindness, language and world, the usual nexus is ruptured. An interval that receives the opacities in order to open art to unlimited encounters, but that does not stop revealing its indeterminations and misfits. From Barja’s works, a series of Brazilian and European theoreticians and artists: Evgene Bavcar, Mercedes Replinger, Adolfo Montejo Navas, Roland Campos, Angélica Madeira, Bené Fonteles and Marília Panitz produced an important body of reflections that accompanies this compilation of records that survived time. It is possible, in this way, to travel here through twenty years of history by means of the projects and installations: “Experiência Tumulto (1985)”, “Cubo Cruz Lápide (1985)”, “O Profeta e a Jaguatirica (1985-86)”, “DO AKD-MICO AO POLE-MICO (1986)”, “Mognus Dei (1990)”, “O Sol de Goethe (1999)”, “São João Beuys (1990)”, “Ser ou não Ser, Ao Gullar (1993)”, “Pega Manet/De Onde Vem A Escuridão (1986)”, “TV Anal (1999)”, “Hermógenes (1999)”, “Obranome (2003)” and “Cultura X Natureza = Barbárie (1998/2005)” Marília Panitz, in her text “Ao que importa, uma resposta”, proposes an itinerary for reading Barja’s works, departing from the concept of equation, so dear to the artist. Angélica Madeira highlights the influence of Surrealism and Dada in this work in which the playful, of a supposedly unpretentious humour, coexists with the gravity of the materials, above all the sheep’s fat which, under the action of light, solidifies and liquefies over the course of the day, causing strangeness and unease. Eygene Bavcar, blind since the age of eleven, sets himself “to the listening of a painting” and plunges into the universe of “Hermógenes” and of “O Sol de Goethe”. Bavcar is interested above all in the white cane, one of the objects that compose “Hermógenes”; it becomes “the invisible canvas, the painting to be created (...) the brush over the darkness”. What Barja paints, in composing the space, is the “difficult path of the invisible”, penetrable, perhaps, by the forms that the artist formulates. Mercedes Replinger, together with Marília Panitz, is the one who leans over the whole of Wagner Barja’s oeuvre. This division does not imply strict separation, for all these themes and concepts appear to a greater or lesser degree in each of the pieces and installations, which represent in themselves an excess and a residue, which unfolds in the following work and generates a continuous process of metamorphoses, thus underlining the open character of artistic creation. To look, in this sense, necessarily implies theorizing, generating a thought that is built with the very movement of the eyes. As Goethe had already pointed out: “The mere looking at things leads to nothing. Every look turns into consideration; every consideration turns into meditation; every meditation into relating; for this reason one may say that it is enough to look with a little attention for us to be already in full theorizing activity” (1). To look with attention is, then, also to listen, since the look that thinks, without doubt, speaks and listens; thus it produces an endless play of exchanges between vision and hearing, between the words that are seen and the images that hear. Reciprocity of the senses, of images and of words, also of feelings and of places.

A dream, however, the beauty of the metaphor, light as sound, allows Barja to lower the pitch of visibility of this installation, displacing the intensity of visual perception to the acoustic. Sound, without doubt, is the quality most detached from the object and from its representation, the one that keeps the greatest distance with respect to visibility, equalling, situating on the same level the seeing and the non-seeing. Literally the artist is pleading for the opening, in the plastic space, of an ocular music. In “O Sol de Goethe” (1990) there is still a limit to visibility which is given by another correspondence also inscribed in the title: the analogy that Goethe establishes between the eye and the sun, as he presents it in the introduction to his well-known Farbenlehre (theory of colours), of 1810. trecho.9: Goethe; indeed, he went further and imagined the existence in the human being of an eye specific for contemplating the sun: the pineal eye, a gland situated below the cranial box which, unlike the eyes caught in the horizontality of everyday becoming, of what offers itself to the gaze, allows us to rise and see the sun face to face, like the eagle of the ancients. The pineal eye is, for Bataille, the confirmation of the human being’s eagerness to raise himself above his earthly condition. That uncontained desire to see the sun face to face would mark, according to the French author, the evolution of man from his inclined, quadruped position
trecho.10: which Beuys represented, his confidence in the possibility of using the energy of the animals to reach the desired unity that, long before, had already been announced, for example, by Schiller when he envied the Greeks’ proximity to nature: “they are what we were; they are what we must become again. We have been nature like them, and our culture must return by the path of reason and freedom to nature”. But the equation reason and nature has only produced destruction. The thing seems to come from olden times, from the beginning: let us listen again to Mephistopheles when he confronts the Creator, this one whom Goethe calls the Lord, and all his creation, and with his finger pointed out marks as the origin of man’s ills this so fateful desire that will lose Him: “Of the sun and of the worlds there is nothing to say, and I only see how mortals weary themselves. The rickety god of the earth remains of the same nature and as extravagant as on the first day. He would live a little better had you not given him that fire of celestial light, which he calls Reason and which he uses only to be more bestial than any beast” (47) .
